# Passenger Rail Corridor Proposal: New York City, NY to Chicago, IL

> **Illustrative estimates: costs, schedules and funding figures in this draft come from an uncalibrated planning model and approximate program parameters. They are not budgets or engineering estimates.**

## Executive Summary

This proposal evaluates three passenger-rail corridor options between New York City, NY and Chicago, IL using 5000 Monte Carlo simulation runs per alternative. The evaluated routes are Alternative 1 (Lake Shore corridor upgrade), Alternative 2 (Pennsylvania corridor upgrade), and Alternative 3 (New direct high-speed alignment). Population served reflects 2020 Census residents within a 10 miles population buffer.

The Pennsylvania corridor upgrade achieves the highest composite score at 86.9 out of 100, the lowest median (P50) cost, the shortest median (P50) schedule, and serves the most population near line at 22.33 million residents. The Lake Shore corridor upgrade scores 83.2 out of 100, while the New direct high-speed alignment scores 69.6 out of 100.

## Corridor Description

The Lake Shore corridor upgrade spans 954 miles with 99.7% share on existing rail, serving 11 stations including New York City, Buffalo, Syracuse, Albany, Utica, Poughkeepsie, Chicago, Cleveland, Toledo, South Bend, and Erie. It passes 22.23 million residents within 10 miles, with 20 river crossings and 20 environmental flag entries.

The Pennsylvania corridor upgrade spans 858 miles with 99.9% share on existing rail, serving 6 stations including New York City, Chicago, Philadelphia, Pittsburgh, Fort Wayne, and Harrisburg. It serves 22.33 million residents within 10 miles, with 11 river crossings and 10 environmental flag entries.

The New direct high-speed alignment is the shortest length route at 743 miles, but features a 23.1% share on existing rail. It serves 2 stations (New York City and Chicago), 16.14 million residents within 10 miles, 5 river crossings, and 7 environmental flag entries.

## Cost and Schedule Range

Costs are illustrative estimates based on per-mile benchmarks from publicly reported US rail projects, not calibrated engineering estimates or budgets. Capital costs and time to opening reflect P10, median (P50), and P90 figures from continuous-aggregate histograms derived from simulation runs.

For the Pennsylvania corridor upgrade, capital costs are $19.7B at P10, $24.3B at median (P50), and $30.2B at P90; time to opening is 13.8 years at P10, 15.8 years at median (P50), and 17.9 years at P90. For the Lake Shore corridor upgrade, capital costs are $20.3B at P10, $25.2B at median (P50), and $31.4B at P90; time to opening is 15.4 years at P10, 17.8 years at median (P50), and 20.3 years at P90. For the New direct high-speed alignment, capital costs are $29.6B at P10, $35.5B at median (P50), and $42.2B at P90; time to opening is 15.9 years at P10, 18.0 years at median (P50), and 20.2 years at P90.

## Funding Strategy

All alternatives are eligible to seek entry into the FRA Corridor Identification and Development Program (Corridor ID) with a $500K federal planning grant amount to fund Step 1 scoping. Core capital grant funding is available via the FRA Federal-State Partnership for Intercity Passenger Rail (National) program up to $3.0B per award, representing 12.3% of median (P50) cost for Alternative 2, 11.9% for Alternative 1, and 8.5% for Alternative 3. Because median (P50) costs exceed $3.0B, capital builds would require multi-award phasing.

Additional grant sources include FRA CRISI funding (capped near $250M, matching 1.0% of median cost for Alternatives 1 and 2, and 0.7% for Alternative 3) and USDOT BUILD grants ($25M cap). Alternative 2 can leverage FRA Federal-State Partnership (Northeast Corridor) grants up to $2.1B (8.5% of median cost) for its 91 miles on the NEC main line, whereas Alternative 1 has a $1.0B (4.0% of median cost) NEC fit. Non-federal match requirements (20% of median cost) can be financed using USDOT Build America Bureau RRIF loans up to $3.0B.

## Risks

Key risks and constraints identified across the alternatives include:

* Governance and Interstate Coordination: Routes span multiple state jurisdictions (5 states for Lake Shore corridor upgrade, 4 states for Pennsylvania corridor upgrade, 2 states for New direct high-speed alignment), requiring formal interstate compacts or multi-state sponsoring entities.
* Greenfield Acquisition and Environmental Impact: The New direct high-speed alignment relies heavily on new right-of-way (23.1% share on existing rail) through mountain structures across Pennsylvania and Ohio.
* Water and Environmental Crossings: Lake Shore corridor upgrade requires navigating 20 river crossings and 20 environmental flag entries, compared to 11 river crossings and 10 flag entries for Pennsylvania corridor upgrade.
* Revenue and Financing Commitments: RRIF loans require dedicated repayment sources, such as state appropriations or farebox revenues, to finance non-federal cost shares ($4.9B for Alternative 2, $5.0B for Alternative 1, and $7.1B for Alternative 3).

## Next Steps

Recommended next steps for project advance include:

* Establish a multi-state governance structure or interstate compact among participating states.
* Apply for $500K in FRA Corridor ID planning funds to complete Step 1 scoping and secure pipeline prioritization for future FSP-National capital awards.
* Formulate a multi-year award phasing plan for the primary capital build to accommodate program award caps.
* Conduct refined engineering studies to update illustrative cost benchmarks and assess real-world right-of-way conditions.
